title: The first approach is not the best approach
description: Why an agent's first idea for how to do something is a starting point, not a decision — and what it costs when nobody checks.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when an agent has committed to its first approach without considering alternatives
Analyze a real case where the first approach was materially worse than an available alternative

contentSections.body: Asked to find every place in a 40-file codebase that calls a deprecated function, an agent immediately starts `grep`-ing files one at a time in a loop, reading each result, deciding whether it's a real match. Forty tool calls later it has an answer. A single `grep -rn` across the whole directory would have found the same answer in one call.

contentSections.question: The agent above never considered the one-call grep. Why not — what's actually missing from how it approached the task, not just from the specific tool it used?
contentSections.answer: **It never generated alternatives before committing.** The model reached for the first plausible approach (loop through files one at a time) and started executing immediately, rather than first asking "what are 2-3 ways to do this, and which is actually cheapest?" A model that's perfectly capable of knowing `grep -rn` exists will still reach for the file-by-file loop if nothing in its process asks it to consider alternatives before committing to the first one.
contentSections.hint: This isn't really about grep specifically — what step in the agent's process was simply never taken?

contentSections.body:
The model didn't lack the knowledge that `grep -rn` exists — asked directly "what's a faster way to search 40 files for a pattern," it would say exactly that. The failure is procedural, not a knowledge gap: **nothing in the agent's process asked it to consider more than one approach before starting.** The first plausible idea became the plan, by default, because "generate alternatives, then pick" isn't something that happens automatically just because a capable model is doing the reasoning.

This matters because the cost compounds with scale. One extra tool call to search a 5-file project barely registers. The same file-by-file habit on a 400-file monorepo is the difference between one grep and four hundred sequential reads — and the agent that skipped comparing approaches has no way to notice this until it's already forty calls deep.
A capable model reaching for its first idea isn't a knowledge gap — it's a missing step. Nothing asked it to compare approaches before committing to one.

An agent tasked with deduplicating 10,000 customer records picks the first approach it thinks of — compare every record to every other record, an O(n²) approach that's 100 million comparisons. A faster approach exists (sort by a normalized key first, then only compare adjacent records) but the agent never weighed it against the first idea.

contentSections.scenario: The O(n²) all-pairs comparison approach on 10,000 records versus the sort-then-compare-adjacent approach.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many comparisons does the sort-based approach need, compared to the ~100 million all-pairs comparisons?
contentSections.explanation: Sorting is O(n log n) — about 10,000 × 14 ≈ 140,000 operations for the sort itself, then one pass comparing each record only to its immediate neighbor: roughly 10,000 comparisons. That's a difference of four orders of magnitude from the all-pairs approach's 100 million — the kind of gap that turns "runs for hours" into "runs in under a second," and it was available the whole time, just never weighed against the first idea.

contentSections.body:
This is the general shape of the cost: **the first approach is usually correct, rarely the cheapest, and the gap between them grows with the size of the problem.** On a small input, an inefficient approach still finishes and nobody notices. On a large input, the same unexamined habit is the difference between a task that completes and one that times out, burns an enormous token or API budget, or gets killed by a rate limit halfway through.

The fix isn't "always find the theoretically optimal approach" — that's its own kind of waste, spending planning effort a simple task didn't need. It's specifically: **before committing, generate at least one genuine alternative and compare them on the dimensions that actually matter for this task** (speed, cost, reliability, how much can go wrong) — which is exactly what the rest of this module builds out.
The first approach is usually correct and rarely the cheapest — and the gap between them grows with problem size, which is exactly when nobody's watching closely enough to catch it.

title: Generating alternatives before committing
description: A concrete pattern for making an agent produce 2-3 genuinely different approaches before picking one, and what makes alternatives genuinely different rather than cosmetic variations.

learningObjectives.text: Design a prompt pattern that forces genuine alternative generation before commitment
Distinguish genuinely different approaches from cosmetic variations of the same one

contentSections.title: Forcing the comparison to actually happen

contentSections.body: "Before doing anything, list a few ways you could approach this" sounds like it should fix the grep problem from lesson one. Asked this way, a lot of agents will produce three options that are all the same idea with the file names changed — which technically satisfies the instruction while doing none of the actual work of comparing approaches.

A prompt pattern that reliably produces genuine alternatives, not cosmetic ones:

```
Before starting, propose 2-3 genuinely different approaches to this task.
For each, state:
- The core mechanism (not just a restatement of the goal)
- Its approximate cost (tool calls, tokens, or time)
- Its main failure mode

Then pick one and state why, in one sentence, referencing the comparison above.
```

The part doing the real work is **"the core mechanism"** — asking specifically what's mechanically different, not just differently worded. "Search file by file" and "search all files at once with a single grep" are mechanistically different (one loop, N calls; one call, no loop). "Search file by file, starting with the largest files" and "search file by file, starting with the smallest files" are the same mechanism with a different order — not a genuine alternative, just a variation.

Asking for alternatives only works if it asks for the core mechanism specifically — otherwise you get the same idea restated three ways, which satisfies the instruction without doing the actual comparison.

contentSections.scenario:
Asked to summarize customer feedback from 200 support tickets, an agent proposes:

A. "Read all 200 tickets in one context window and summarize them together."
B. "Read all 200 tickets, but read the urgent ones first."
C. "Cluster tickets by topic first using embeddings, summarize each cluster separately, then combine the cluster summaries."
contentSections.question: Which pair is a genuine alternative — mechanistically different, not just reordered?

options.label: A and C — one context-window pass versus clustering-then-per-cluster summarization
A and B — reading all tickets versus reading urgent ones first

feedback.a-c: Right. A processes everything in one pass with no structural grouping; C introduces an entirely different mechanism (embedding-based clustering, then per-cluster processing) with different cost characteristics (extra embedding calls, but each summarization call handles a smaller, more coherent chunk) and a different failure mode (a bad cluster boundary versus one context window getting too large to hold everything).
feedback.a-b: A and B do the exact same thing — read every ticket, summarize — just in a different order. Ordering by urgency doesn't change the mechanism at all; it's the same approach with a different starting point, exactly the cosmetic-variation trap this lesson is naming.

contentSections.concept: A genuine alternative changes the *mechanism* — how the work actually gets done, what it costs, and how it can fail. A cosmetic variation changes only the order, naming, or surface framing while the underlying mechanism stays identical.

contentSections.body:
A quick test for whether two proposed approaches are genuinely different: **if you deleted the parts of each description that just restate the goal, would what's left describe a different process?** "Read tickets and summarize, urgent first" versus "read tickets and summarize, all at once" — strip the goal restatement ("summarize the tickets") and what's left is just an ordering choice, not a different process. "Read tickets and summarize" versus "cluster tickets by topic, then summarize each cluster" — strip the goal restatement and what's left is genuinely two different pipelines.

A model asked to generate alternatives will sometimes produce cosmetic variations specifically because it's easier and still technically answers the prompt. Explicitly asking for the *mechanism* per option — not just the option's name — is what forces the real comparison lesson one showed was missing.
Strip the goal restatement from each proposed approach — if what's left still describes a different process, it's genuine; if what's left is empty or just an ordering, it's cosmetic.

title: Cheap checks before expensive work
description: Running a fast, low-cost probe to validate an approach's core assumption before spending the full budget on it.

learningObjectives.text: Design a cheap validation check that tests an approach's core assumption before full execution
Identify the specific assumption a cheap check should target for a given approach

contentSections.title: Testing the assumption, not the whole plan

contentSections.body: An agent decides the fastest way to answer "which of these 500 product pages mention a discontinued ingredient" is to fetch and scan all 500 pages. Before doing that, it fetches and scans 5. All 5 have the ingredient listed in the same predictable spot in the HTML (a `<div class="ingredients">` block) — meaning a targeted parse, not a full-page scan, will work for the other 495 too, at a fraction of the cost per page.

contentSections.scenario: The agent checked 5 pages before committing to a parsing strategy for the remaining 495, rather than either scanning all 500 in full or guessing at the HTML structure without checking any.
contentSections.question: What did the 5-page check actually verify that made it worth the small upfront cost?

options.label: Whether the approach's core assumption (ingredients always appear in a predictable, parseable location) holds — cheaply, on a sample, before betting the full budget on it
Whether the website was online and responding
Nothing meaningful — 5 pages is too small a sample to prove anything

feedback.assumption: Right. The expensive approach (targeted parsing instead of full scans) only pays off if the assumption behind it — predictable structure — is actually true. Checking 5 real pages tests exactly that assumption, cheaply, before committing the other 495 pages' processing to a strategy that might not have worked.
feedback.uptime: The check does incidentally confirm the site responds, but that's not what it's actually verifying — the real target is the structural assumption the cheaper approach depends on, not basic availability.
feedback.too-small: Five isn't a rigorous statistical sample, but that's not the bar here — the check isn't proving the assumption is universally true, it's cheaply surfacing whether it's *plausible enough* to bet the cheap approach on, with a plan to notice and adapt if later pages break the pattern.

contentSections.mechanism: A cheap check exists to validate the specific assumption an approach's cost savings depend on, using a small, fast sample — not to prove the whole task will succeed, and not to check something unrelated like basic connectivity.

contentSections.body: A cheap check tests the one assumption an approach's savings depend on, on a small sample, before betting the full-scale budget on it — and it only pays off when the full-scale savings are large enough to be worth the check's own cost.

contentSections.title: Picking the right thing to check

contentSections.body: An agent planning to use a third-party API's bulk endpoint (cheaper per-record than the single-record endpoint) checks whether the API is reachable — it is — and commits to the bulk approach for 10,000 records. Two thousand records in, the bulk endpoint starts silently dropping records over a certain batch size, which "is the API reachable" never would have caught.

contentSections.question: This is a real cheap check before an expensive commitment. What's wrong with it?

options.label: It checks the wrong assumption — API reachability, not the actual thing the bulk approach's savings depend on (that bulk imports of this size behave correctly)
Health checks are always a bad idea before a bulk operation

feedback.wrong-assumption: Right. A health check confirms the API is up — true, and irrelevant to whether the bulk endpoint handles a 10,000-record batch correctly. The actual assumption the bulk approach depends on is 'this endpoint handles batches of this size without silently dropping records,' which a `/health` ping can't tell you anything about.
feedback.no-health: Health checks are fine and often useful — the problem isn't that a health check ran, it's that it was the *only* check, and it verified something unrelated to the specific risk in this approach.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Picking the right thing to check means identifying the actual mechanism the cost savings depend on — here, correct behavior at scale, not basic connectivity — and testing that specifically, ideally on a batch size close to (but smaller than) the real one, e.g. a 50-record test bulk import with an exact record-count verification on the far side.

contentSections.body: The question to ask when designing a cheap check: **"if this approach is going to fail me at full scale, what's the specific way it would fail, and can I trigger that failure mode cheaply on a small sample?"** For a structure assumption (lesson's first half), that's sampling a few real items. For a scale assumption (this example), that's running a smaller-but-still-nontrivial batch and verifying the count matches, not just pinging that the endpoint exists. A cheap check that verifies something true but irrelevant gives false confidence — worse in a way than no check at all, because it looks like due diligence was done.

Design the cheap check around the specific way the approach would actually fail at scale — not around whatever's easiest to check. A check that verifies something true but irrelevant is false confidence, not due diligence.

title: Knowing when to abandon an approach
description: Distinguishing an approach that's slow-but-working from one that's genuinely failing, and setting real abandonment criteria before starting rather than deciding in the moment.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a slow-but-working approach from one that is genuinely failing
Set concrete abandonment criteria for an approach before executing it

contentSections.body: An agent trying every combination of two API parameters to find one that returns the expected result is on attempt 40 of a search space of 60. It's slow. It's also making steady, visible progress — 39 ruled-out combinations closer to done than it was at attempt 1. Abandoning now would throw away nearly all of that progress for nothing.

contentSections.scenario: Four agents, each 15 minutes into a task that was estimated to take 5.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuine signals to abandon the current approach, versus just being slower than hoped?

items.label: It's tried 40 of 60 possible combinations, ruling more out each time — 15 minutes in, but visibly closer to done
It's called the same API endpoint with the same arguments 6 times in a row and gotten the identical error each time
It found the answer on the 3rd of 10 planned data sources and is now spending time re-verifying it 7 more times for no new information
It's processed 15 of 200 records — slower than estimated, but each one succeeds and the rate is stable

explanation.narrowing: Not a signal to abandon — this is genuinely converging, just slower than the estimate. The estimate being wrong isn't the same as the approach being wrong.
explanation.repeat: A real signal — six identical failures with zero new information is the stuck-loop pattern: nothing is changing, so nothing about continuing the same way is going to produce a different result.
explanation.diminishing: A real signal, of a different kind — the goal was already achieved on attempt 3; everything since has been re-confirming a known answer instead of stopping. This is a case for recognizing the task is done, not that the approach failed, but it's the same underlying skill: noticing when continuing stops producing value.
explanation.slow-progress: Not a signal to abandon — a stable success rate that's merely slower than hoped is a scheduling problem, not an approach problem. Abandoning here throws away working progress to chase a different approach with no evidence it'll be faster.

contentSections.synthesis: The dividing line isn't speed — it's whether continuing is producing new information or new progress. Steady narrowing, even if slow, is progress. Identical repeated failures and continuing past an already-achieved goal both mean continuing adds nothing, which is the real signal, not the clock.

contentSections.body: Slow isn't the same as stuck. The real signal to abandon is whether continuing is still producing new progress or new information — not how much time has passed.

contentSections.title: Setting the criteria before you need them

contentSections.body: Deciding whether to abandon an approach is much easier to get right when the decision was made in advance, with a clear head, than in the moment — mid-task, having already sunk time into it, an agent (and a person) is prone to exactly the sunk-cost reasoning that keeps a failing approach running long past when it should have stopped.

Decide the abandonment criteria before starting, not mid-task — a repeated-identical-failure count, a cost ceiling, and a progress checkpoint, all set while it's still easy to think clearly about what the task is worth.

title: Recording why an approach was chosen
description: Logging the comparison, not just the choice — what a reviewer actually needs to understand a decision after the fact.

learningObjectives.text: Design a decision record that captures the comparison behind a strategy choice, not just the outcome

contentSections.title: The decision without the reasoning is useless later

contentSections.body: A week later, someone asks why the customer-dedup agent used the sort-and-compare-adjacent approach instead of a fuzzy-matching library. The agent's log says: "Approach: sort-and-compare." That's the what. Nobody kept the why — was fuzzy matching considered and rejected, or never considered at all? There's no way to tell from this log, which means there's no way to know whether revisiting the decision is worth anyone's time.

contentSections.question: This is a real log entry from a completed agent run. What's missing that a reviewer would actually need?

options.label: What alternatives were considered and why this one was chosen over them
The exact timestamp of completion

feedback.no-alternatives: Right. This log says what happened and that it worked, but nothing about the decision itself — what else was considered, on what basis this one won, what would have to change for a different choice to be right. Without that, nobody reviewing this later can tell whether the choice still makes sense as circumstances change, or whether it was even a real decision versus just the first idea (lesson one's problem, recurring here as an audit trail gap).
feedback.no-timestamp: A timestamp is nice-to-have logging hygiene, but it's not what makes this log useless for understanding the decision — the actual gap is the missing comparison, not a missing field like this.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A decision record that only states the outcome answers "what happened" but not "was this a good decision, and would it still be one if something changed" — which is exactly the question someone reviewing it later actually has.

contentSections.body:
A decision record worth keeping has three parts, corresponding to lessons two through four of this module:

1. **What alternatives were considered** — the genuine ones from lesson two, with their core mechanism, not a token list of options that were never really weighed.
2. **What the cheap check (if any) showed** — from lesson three, if a check ran, what it found and how that shaped the choice.
3. **The deciding factor, stated concretely** — not "this seemed best" but "chosen because it's O(n log n) versus O(n²), and the dataset is large enough that this dominates."

```json
{
  "task": "deduplicate customer records",
  "alternatives_considered": [
    {"approach": "all-pairs comparison", "cost": "~100M comparisons, O(n\u00b2)"},
    {"approach": "sort by normalized key, compare adjacent", "cost": "~10K comparisons, O(n log n)"}
  ],
  "cheap_check": "sampled 50 records, confirmed normalized key produces stable, comparable sort order",
  "chosen": "sort-and-compare-adjacent",
  "deciding_factor": "cost gap of ~4 orders of magnitude at this dataset size (10,000 records) dominates the decision",
  "result": "success, 340 duplicates found"
}
```

This costs almost nothing to produce — the model already did this reasoning to make the choice; the record just asks it to write down what it already figured out, instead of discarding it the moment the decision is made.

A useful decision record captures the alternatives, what any cheap check showed, and the concrete deciding factor — the reasoning already happened; the record just keeps it instead of throwing it away.

contentSections.title: When the record earns its cost

contentSections.body: Not every choice needs a full decision record — an agent picking between two nearly-identical ways to format a log line doesn't need an alternatives-considered writeup any more than lesson two of the previous module's stock-price lookup needed a plan.

contentSections.scenario: An agent makes several strategy choices in one run: which search approach to use for a research task, which log format to use for its own internal debug output, which database migration strategy to use for a production schema change, and which variable name to use in a helper function.
contentSections.question: Which of these choices are worth a real decision record?

items.label: Which search approach to use for the research task (multiple genuinely different options, real cost difference)
Which migration strategy to use for a production schema change (expensive to reverse, real stakeholder interest in why)
Which internal debug log format to use
Which variable name to use inside a helper function

explanation.search: Worth recording — this is exactly module 2's real-alternatives case, with a genuine cost difference and enough consequence that someone might reasonably ask about it later.
explanation.migration: Worth recording — expensive to reverse if wrong, and the kind of choice a teammate reviewing the change would specifically want to understand, not just see the result of.
explanation.logformat: Not worth a decision record — low stakes, easily changed later, and nobody is going to ask 'why did you format the debug log this way' the way they'd ask about a migration strategy.
explanation.varname: Not worth a decision record — trivially reversible, no real alternative comparison happened or should happen, purely a matter of local style.

contentSections.synthesis: The same proportionality judgment as plan-first (an earlier module) and cheap checks (this module's lesson three): record the reasoning when the choice was genuinely consequential and expensive to revisit, and skip the overhead when it wasn't — recording every trivial choice just buries the decisions that actually mattered under noise nobody will ever read.

contentSections.body: Record the reasoning when a choice is consequential and costly to revisit — skip it for low-stakes, easily-reversed choices, or the record becomes noise nobody reads instead of a trail worth having.

title: Evaluate seven strategy selections
description: Seven drills applying this module's toolkit — genuine alternatives, cheap checks, abandonment signals, decision records — to new scenarios.

learningObjectives.text: Apply alternative-generation, cheap-check design, abandonment judgment, and decision-recording to new strategy-selection scenarios

contentSections.body: The same toolkit from the five lessons, applied to strategy choices you haven't seen yet — including a couple that need this phase's earlier decomposition skills too.

The habit worth keeping: before committing to the first workable idea, name a genuinely different alternative, know what you'd cheaply check to validate the risky assumption, decide in advance what would make you abandon it, and write down the deciding factor while you still remember it.

title: Add strategy selection to your agent
description: Extend the plan-then-execute agent from the previous module's lab so that, before executing, it considers genuine alternatives and logs its reasoning for the choice — real strategy selection, not a first-idea default.

learningObjectives.text: Add genuine alternative generation and a logged strategy decision to a working agent

contentSections.body: The previous module's agent planned its steps before executing, but the plan itself was still whatever the model's first idea produced. This lab adds the missing layer: before committing to an approach for at least one real step, the agent has to generate genuine alternatives, weigh them, and log why it picked what it picked.

contentSections.title: Genuine alternatives, weighed and logged
contentSections.brief: Using the plan-then-execute agent from the previous lab (or a new task if that one doesn't have a step with real strategy alternatives), find at least one step in its plan where more than one genuinely different approach exists — a search strategy, a data-processing method, an API usage pattern. Build a strategy-selection layer that generates 2-3 real alternatives for that step (mechanism, cost, failure mode each), runs a cheap check if one is warranted, picks one with a stated deciding factor, and logs the full comparison.
contentSections.deliverable: The strategy-selection code, a real run's decision record showing genuine (not cosmetic) alternatives with their mechanisms and costs, evidence of a cheap check if the approach warranted one, and a short writeup of what would have happened if the agent had just gone with its first idea instead — a real comparison, not a hypothetical.

stages.title: Find a step with genuine alternatives
stages.instructions: Identify a step in your agent's plan where at least two mechanistically different approaches exist — not two orderings of the same approach. Apply lesson two's strip-the-goal-restatement test to confirm they're genuinely different before proceeding.
stages.checkpoint: Two or more candidate approaches for one real step, each passing the genuine-versus-cosmetic test.

stages.title: Build the alternative-generation and comparison prompt
stages.instructions: Write the prompt pattern from lesson two — mechanism, cost, failure mode per option — and generate real alternatives for your chosen step. Decide, per lesson three, whether a cheap check is warranted here (is there an assumption the cost savings of one option depend on, cheap to test on a sample?), and if so, implement and run it.
stages.checkpoint: Real, non-cosmetic alternatives generated, each with a stated mechanism/cost/failure-mode, plus a cheap check if the situation warranted one.

stages.title: Pick, execute, and set abandonment criteria
stages.instructions: Pick an approach with a concrete, stated deciding factor (not "this seemed best"). Before executing, set lesson four's abandonment criteria for it (identical-failure count, cost ceiling, or progress checkpoint — whichever is relevant). Execute it for real.
stages.checkpoint: A concrete deciding factor recorded before execution, explicit abandonment criteria set before execution, and a real execution run.

stages.title: Log the decision record and compare against the road not taken
stages.instructions: Produce the full decision record per lesson five's shape. Then honestly estimate what would have happened with the rejected alternative — would it genuinely have been worse, by how much, and is your estimate grounded in something concrete (an actual smaller-scale test, a real cost calculation) rather than an assumption.
stages.checkpoint: A complete decision record, plus a grounded (not hand-waved) comparison against the approach that wasn't chosen.

rubric.criterion: The alternatives are genuinely different, not cosmetic
rubric.meets: Each alternative changes the actual mechanism (per lesson two's test), not just the ordering or naming of the same underlying process.

rubric.criterion: A cheap check ran where the situation warranted one
rubric.meets: If an alternative's cost savings depended on an assumption, that assumption was tested on a small sample before committing — or there's a stated reason none was needed.

rubric.criterion: The chosen approach has a concrete, stated deciding factor
rubric.meets: The reason for the choice references the actual comparison (cost, reliability, risk) rather than a vague 'this seemed best.'

rubric.criterion: Abandonment criteria were set before execution, not improvised mid-run
rubric.meets: A specific, concrete threshold (failure count, cost ceiling, or progress checkpoint) was written down before the approach started executing.

rubric.criterion: The decision record is complete
rubric.meets: Alternatives considered, cheap-check result (if any), and the deciding factor are all present in a structured, reviewable form.

rubric.criterion: The road-not-taken comparison is grounded, not hand-waved
rubric.meets: The estimate of what the rejected alternative would have cost is based on something concrete — a calculation, a smaller test — not an unverified assumption.

contentSections.body: Strategy selection isn't a separate skill from decomposition — it's what happens at the moment a step in the plan could genuinely be done more than one way, and this lab is the difference between an agent that has a plan and one that chose it.

title: Checkpoint — Choosing an Approach
description: Ungraded retrieval: 4 from this module, 4 from Decomposition (the previous module), 2 from further back in Agent Foundations.

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — Choosing an Approach
contentSections.framing: No grade, no timer. Answer from memory before scrolling back.

questions.prompt: An agent's first idea for a task is usually correct. What's the actual problem with executing it without comparison?

options.label: It's rarely the cheapest, and the gap to a better approach grows with problem size — exactly when nobody notices until it's too late
The first idea is usually wrong
There's no real problem — models always pick well

questions.explanation: The grep and dedup examples both showed a correct-but-expensive first idea, where the gap to a cheaper approach only became a real problem at scale.

questions.prompt: Two proposed approaches for the same task differ only in the order they process items, with the same underlying mechanism. Are they genuine alternatives?

options.label: No — strip the goal restatement from each and what's left is just an ordering, not a different process
Yes — different orderings always count as different approaches

questions.explanation: Lesson two's ticket-summary example showed exactly this trap — reading urgent-first versus reading in original order is the same mechanism, not a real alternative.

questions.prompt: A cheap check before committing to an approach should test what, specifically?

options.label: The specific assumption the approach's cost savings actually depend on
Whatever is easiest and fastest to check

questions.explanation: The health-check example in lesson three showed a cheap check that verified something true but irrelevant — false confidence rather than real due diligence.

questions.prompt: What's the real signal that an approach should be abandoned — slowness, or something else?

options.label: Whether continuing is still producing new progress or new information — not how much time has passed
Any task that's taking longer than originally estimated

questions.explanation: Lesson four's evidence-stack distinguished steady-but-slow narrowing (keep going) from identical repeated failures (stuck, abandon) — speed alone didn't tell them apart.

questions.prompt: What makes a step's completion condition genuinely checkable?

options.label: A concrete target, a mechanical check, and a binary answer
A detailed, thorough description of the work
Approval from the model that wrote the step

questions.explanation: Worth reconnecting here — this module's cheap checks and abandonment criteria both depend on the same kind of concrete, mechanically-verifiable condition, applied to a strategy decision instead of a plan step.

questions.prompt: Two plan steps don't read each other's output but write to the same file. Are they safe to run concurrently?

options.label: No — shared mutable state makes them dependent even without direct data flow
Yes — no data flow between them means they're independent

questions.explanation: A real dependency needs checking both data flow and shared state — the same kind of "looks fine on the surface, isn't" trap this module's cheap-check lesson names for cost assumptions.

questions.prompt: A plan fails at one step because of a wrong local assumption (a field moved location in an API response). What's the right-sized response?

options.label: A local patch to that step — nothing about the failure calls the completed earlier steps into question
A full replan from the beginning, since something about the environment changed

options.label: A goal — the outcome, with no single tool call that achieves it directly
A step — specific enough to hand directly to a tool

questions.explanation: Still the foundational vocabulary this whole phase builds on — a strategy decision (this module) still has to resolve down to genuinely checkable steps (previous module) before it means anything executable.

options.label: A code-level tally of actual results that gates any success claim, not a stronger prompt instruction
Asking the model to double-check more carefully

options.label: The number or order of steps depends on what earlier steps discover
It uses more than one tool

title: Asking an agent to check its own work
description: What a self-review pass actually is — a second inference pass on the same output — and why what it's asked to check about matters more than whether it's asked at all.

learningObjectives.text: Describe what a self-review step mechanically is: a second model call examining the first pass's output
Write a self-review prompt that asks about specific, checkable properties rather than a global verdict
Evaluate whether a given self-review prompt is likely to catch anything the first pass missed

contentSections.body: An agent writes a SQL migration script, and the very next thing your code does is ask the same Claude call: "does this look correct?" It says yes. It said yes on the version with a typo in the column name, too — the model that made the mistake is the same model being asked whether there's a mistake in it.

contentSections.scenario:
Two review prompts, run right after an agent writes a Python function that processes uploaded files:

A. "Does this look correct? Answer yes or no."
B. "Check specifically: does every code path that opens a file also close it? Does every function argument get validated before use? List any violations found, or say NONE_FOUND."
contentSections.question: Which is actually more likely to catch a real bug?

options.label: B — it asks about specific, checkable properties
A — a direct yes/no question forces a clear answer

feedback.specific: Right. "Does every opened file get closed" gives the model something concrete to actually trace through the code and fail on. A yes/no "looks correct?" invites the same reflex that produced a first-pass mistake to also produce a confident approval of it — nothing in the question forces the model to check anything in particular.
feedback.vague: A forced yes/no answer isn't the same as a forced check. The model can answer "yes" to A without tracing a single code path — nothing in the question requires it to. B's specificity is what makes it checkable, not B's phrasing being a question at all.

contentSections.concept: A self-review prompt is only as useful as what it actually asks about. A global "does this look correct?" invites a global "looks fine." Naming specific properties to check — resource leaks, unvalidated input, an off-by-one boundary — gives the review something concrete to fail on, whether the answer comes back clean or not.

contentSections.body: A self-review step is a second pass on the same output — and it's only as useful as the specific properties it's asked to check, not whether it's asked at all.

contentSections.title: Same conversation or a fresh one

contentSections.body: A team's "review step" is a single extra line appended to the same conversation the agent used to write the code: "Are you sure?" The model, still holding the same context that produced the mistake, says yes — it hasn't been given anything new to reconsider, just a nudge to reconsider the same thing.

contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this "review" step?

options.label: It's still the same conversation, with the same reasoning already in context — nothing new has been introduced for the model to check against
Nothing — appending a follow-up question is a legitimate way to trigger review

feedback.same-context: Right. The full message history — including whatever reasoning led to the mistake — is still sitting in context. "Are you sure?" doesn't hand the model a new fact or a new lens; it just asks it to restate its confidence in what it already committed to, which is exactly the setup that produces agreement rather than discovery.
feedback.fine: The mechanism matters here: a follow-up question inside the same conversation gives the model no new information to check the earlier answer against. It can only re-derive the same answer from the same premises — which is a different thing from actually being checked.

contentSections.flawExplanation: There are two real modes for a self-review call, and this is neither cleanly: same-context continuation (the model still holds its own reasoning, so it mainly catches slips it would readily admit if asked precisely) versus a fresh call given only the finished artefact with no reasoning trail attached. A vague "are you sure?" inside the same context gets the worst of both — no new information, and no forcing function to look at anything specific.

contentSections.body:
Two real modes, not one:

**Same-context continuation** — the review call still has the whole conversation, including the model's own reasoning. Useful for catching slips a specific, narrow question can surface ("did you handle the empty-file case?"), because the model doesn't have to re-derive context, just re-check one thing against context it still holds.

**Fresh call on the artefact alone** — a new call, no conversation history, given only the finished code or output and asked to assess it cold. This removes the risk of the review inheriting the first pass's framing, but it still isn't independent verification in the strong sense — it's still the same model's judgment, just without the specific reasoning trail attached. Lesson three in this module is about the next step up: not judging the artefact by reading it, but running it and checking the actual result.

A vague follow-up in the same conversation gives the model nothing new to check against. A fresh call on the artefact alone removes the inherited framing, but it's still judgment by reading, not verification by running — that's the next lesson.

title: Why self-review often just agrees
description: The actual mechanism behind self-review's blind spot — the same reasoning path that produced a mistake reviewing it, plus a training bias toward agreeable answers — and the two cheap levers that measurably help without becoming full verification.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the mechanism that makes same-source self-review likely to agree with its own earlier output
Identify which changes to a self-review setup genuinely increase what it catches

contentSections.title: The number that should worry you

contentSections.body: A team ran same-context self-review on 50 agent-generated SQL queries before running them against production. The review flagged 2 as buggy. A manual audit of the same 50 queries afterward found 11 that were actually wrong. Nine slipped straight past the check that was supposed to catch them.

contentSections.scenario: The self-review step above ran on the same model, in the same conversation, right after the queries were generated — and still missed 9 of 11 real bugs.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism, not just "the model isn't good enough"?

options.label: The review pass reasons from the same premises that produced the mistake, and models are trained toward agreeable, confirming responses unless explicitly pushed to find fault
The model simply isn't capable of finding SQL bugs
Fifty queries is too small a sample to draw any conclusion from

feedback.same-premises: Right. A model reviewing output it just produced, in the same context, starts from the same assumptions that led it there in the first place — if it believed a JOIN condition was correct while writing it, nothing about being asked to look again changes that belief. On top of that, models trained with human feedback tend toward agreeable, confirming responses by default; "does this look right?" gets answered the way a person answers "do I look fine?" unless the prompt explicitly demands fault-finding.
feedback.not-capable: The same model, given the actual bad query cold — with no memory of having written it, and asked specifically to find the bug — catches a meaningfully higher share of the same errors. The capability is there; what's missing in same-context self-review is a reason for the model to distrust its own prior output.
feedback.sample-size: Fifty is a reasonable sample for a rough estimate, and the gap here (2 caught vs. 11 real) is large enough that sample noise alone doesn't explain it away — teams that run this at larger scale see the same pattern hold.

contentSections.mechanism: Same-context self-review inherits two things from the pass that produced the mistake: the same reasoning that led to the wrong belief in the first place, and a general trained tendency toward confirming rather than contradicting a prior answer. Neither goes away just because you asked a follow-up question — removing either one measurably changes what gets caught.

contentSections.body: This isn't a claim that models can't find bugs — it's a claim about which bugs a specific setup can find. Same-context self-review is good at catching things the model would readily flag if you pointed at them directly (an obviously unclosed bracket, a variable used before assignment), because noticing those doesn't require distrusting the earlier reasoning, just spotting a local slip. It's bad at catching things the model was confidently, systematically wrong about — a JOIN that silently drops rows, a date comparison that's off by a timezone — because catching those requires the review to contradict a belief the same reasoning chain just committed to.
Same-context self-review inherits the same premises and the same agreeable-by-default training bias as the pass that produced the mistake — it catches local slips, not systematic wrong beliefs.

Two changes to the setup above, tested separately: running the review as a fresh call with no memory of having written the query, framed as "find the bug in this query" rather than "does this look right"; and, separately, keeping the same context but adding "assume there is at least one bug — find it." Both catch more than the original. Neither catches as much as running the query against real data and checking the actual result.

contentSections.scenario: The self-review setup for the SQL queries above, considered as separate levers you could pull.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely increases the odds a self-review step catches a real mistake?

items.label: Running the review as a fresh call with no memory of authorship, rather than continuing the same conversation
Explicitly telling the model to assume a bug exists and find it, rather than asking an open "does this look right"
Rewording "does this look right?" as "are you absolutely sure this is right?"
Running the exact same self-review prompt twice and taking the majority answer
Actually executing the query against real or representative data and comparing the output to what's expected

explanation.fresh-call: Real lever — removing the memory of authorship removes the reason to defer to a prior conclusion, even though it's still the same underlying model.
explanation.adversarial-framing: Real lever — an explicit instruction to find fault gives the model a concrete goal that a vague "does this look right" doesn't.
explanation.second-opinion-phrasing: Not a real lever — this is the same question with more words. It doesn't change what the model is being asked to check, so it doesn't change what it's likely to catch.
explanation.same-model-twice: Not a real lever — asking the same model the same question twice, with the same context and the same biases, tends to produce the same answer twice. Repetition isn't independence.
explanation.run-it: The strongest lever of all, and the subject of the next lesson — comparing an actual executed result to an actual expectation doesn't depend on the model's judgment at all.

contentSections.synthesis: Fresh context and adversarial framing both measurably help, because they remove one of the two things same-context self-review inherits from the original pass. Neither is as strong as removing judgment from the check entirely — verifying against what the artefact actually does, not what a model believes about it.

contentSections.body: Two cheap improvements, worth using even when a full independent check isn't practical: run the review as a fresh call rather than a conversation continuation, and give it an explicit adversarial framing ("find the bug" rather than "does this look right"). Neither turns self-review into verification. Both are strictly better than the vague, same-context version most teams reach for first, and cost nothing extra beyond a slightly different prompt and call structure.
Fresh context and an explicit adversarial framing both help, cheaply — but the strongest fix is removing the model's judgment from the check entirely, which is where the next lesson goes.

title: Independent verification against the artefact
description: Checking what a model believes about its output versus checking what the output actually does — the difference between narrating a check and running one — with a real verification harness worked through step by step.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish verification that re-reads the model's own description of its work from verification that inspects the artefact's real behavior
Build a verification step that executes an artefact against real or test data and compares actual output to an expected result

contentSections.title: Narrating a check versus running one

contentSections.body: An agent writes a script that converts a folder of customer records from one schema to another. Asked to verify its work, it re-reads its own explanation of what the script does, confirms the explanation matches the original request, and reports success. The script has never actually been run.

contentSections.scenario:
Two things a verification step could do after the schema-conversion script is written:

A. Re-read the model's own explanation of what the script does, and confirm that explanation matches the request.
B. Run the script against a sample of real (or realistic fixture) records, and compare the actual converted output field-by-field to what the new schema requires.
contentSections.question: Which one is genuine verification?

options.label: B — it checks what the artefact actually does, independent of what anyone believes it does
A — confirming the explanation matches the request is still a real check

feedback.artefact: Right. A's check never touches the actual behavior of the script — it compares one piece of the model's own text (the explanation) to another (the request), and both were produced by the same reasoning that might have gotten the conversion logic wrong in the first place. B produces a fact about the world (the actual converted output) that's true or false independent of anyone's belief about it.
feedback.narrative: This is the same trap as same-context self-review, one level up: comparing a description of the work to a description of the goal never executes the work. A script's explanation can be perfectly accurate about what the author *intended* while the code itself has a bug the explanation doesn't mention.

contentSections.concept: **Independent verification** means checking what an artefact actually does — run it, read its real output, compare that output to a real expectation — rather than checking what anyone (the model included) says it does. The artefact's behavior doesn't care what the explanation claims; that's exactly what makes checking it a genuine test rather than a restatement.

contentSections.body: Independent verification runs the artefact and compares its actual output to a real expectation — it doesn't compare one piece of the model's text to another, which is a restatement wearing a check's clothing.

The pattern above needs to become real code, not just a principle — specifically, a way to run an agent's generated script against a fixture, capture the actual output, and produce a pass/fail with the specific mismatches named.

contentSections.problem: Build a verification harness for the schema-conversion script: run it against a known fixture, diff the actual output against a known-correct expected result, and produce a specific pass/fail.

steps.label: Load a fixture with a known-correct expected result
steps.why: The fixture and its expected output have to be built once, by a human or from a known-good prior conversion — this is the ground truth the check compares against, and it's the one part of the harness that can't come from the model that wrote the script.

steps.label: Run the actual script, in an isolated context
steps.why: The script has to actually execute, on real data, in a context where a bug can genuinely fail (a sandbox, not a description of what the sandbox would show) — otherwise this collapses back into narrating what the code should do.

steps.label: Diff actual against expected, field by field
steps.why: A field-by-field diff produces a specific, actionable list — which record, which field, what was expected versus what came out — instead of a single pass/fail bit that tells you nothing about where to look.

steps.label: Report pass/fail with the specifics, not a summary
steps.why: The point of running the check is to get something more useful than the model's opinion — a concrete list of exactly what's wrong (or confirmation that nothing is) is what makes the result worth acting on.

faded.problem: Same pattern, different artefact: verifying a report-generation agent's output, which should compute total revenue per region from a fixture dataset of orders.

blanks.prompt: What does the ground-truth expected result have to be built from?
blanks.answer: a fixture with a known-correct expected total, built independently of the agent (by hand or from a prior trusted computation)
accept: a fixture with a pre-computed correct answer

blanks.prompt: What has to actually happen to the report-generation code, not just be described?
blanks.answer: it has to actually run against the fixture orders and produce real computed totals
accept: run the report generator on the fixture

blanks.prompt: What should the diff produce instead of a single pass/fail bit?
blanks.answer: a specific list of which region's total was wrong and by how much
accept: per-region mismatches with expected vs actual

faded.why: The procedure doesn't change with the artefact: a ground-truth fixture built independently of the thing being checked, a real execution against it, and a specific diff — not a summary — as the result.

contentSections.procedure: 1. Build a fixture with a known-correct expected result, independent of the artefact being checked. 2. Actually execute the artefact against the fixture. 3. Diff the real output against the expected result at the level of detail that makes a failure actionable. 4. Report pass/fail with the specifics, not a summary.

contentSections.body: A verification harness needs a ground-truth fixture built independently of the artefact, a real execution, and a specific diff — the fixture is the one piece the artefact's own author can't produce for you.

title: Critic and worker as separate roles
description: Splitting generation and review into genuinely separate calls with different system prompts and no shared context — and the specific way a leaky wiring quietly turns a critic back into self-review.

learningObjectives.text: Design a critic system prompt that's structurally independent from the worker that produced the artefact
Identify when a generator/critic setup has accidentally leaked context that undermines the critic's independence

contentSections.body: Same underlying model, two calls: one instructed only to produce a piece of marketing copy, the other given nothing but the finished copy and instructed only to attack it — find the overclaim, the vague benefit, the sentence a lawyer would flag. Neither call knows the other exists.

contentSections.intro: Assemble a critic system prompt for reviewing agent-generated marketing copy, field by field.

fields.prompt: How should the critic call be structured relative to the call that generated the copy?

options.label: As a continuation of the same conversation, so it has full context
As a separate call, given only the finished copy — no conversation history, no reasoning trail

feedback.continuation: This is exactly the same-context problem from earlier in this module — the critic inherits the generator's framing and reasoning, which is the thing most likely to make it agree instead of attack.
feedback.separate: Right — a clean call with no shared history means the critic isn't starting from any of the generator's assumptions about what the copy is trying to do.

fields.prompt: What should the critic's system prompt actually instruct?

options.label: "Review this copy and give feedback"
"Find every overclaim, vague benefit, and unsupportable statement. Assume at least one exists."

feedback.generic: This is the same vague-review problem from lesson one — "give feedback" doesn't force the model to look for anything in particular.
feedback.adversarial: Right — naming specific categories of flaw to hunt for, and assuming one exists, gives the critic a concrete adversarial job rather than an open-ended opinion.

fields.prompt: What should the critic actually produce?

options.label: A paragraph of general impressions
A structured verdict: a list of specific flaws (or NONE_FOUND), each tied to the exact sentence it applies to

feedback.prose: General impressions are hard for downstream code to act on and easy for the critic itself to hedge into vague approval — the same problem a global "does this look right?" has.
feedback.structured: Right — a structured list, each flaw tied to a specific sentence, is both actionable by the generator revising the copy and checkable by a human skimming the critic's output.

contentSections.synthesis: A critic worth the extra call is a separate call (no shared context with the generator), given an explicit adversarial instruction naming what to hunt for, and required to produce a structured, specific verdict rather than a paragraph of impressions.

contentSections.body: A critic earns its independence from three things: a separate call with no shared context, an explicit adversarial instruction, and a structured output tied to specifics rather than a vibe.

contentSections.title: Wiring the two together without leaking context

contentSections.body: A team's "critic" call looks separate on paper — a different system prompt, a different function — but the code that wires it up passes the entire prior conversation, including the generator's own reasoning about why the copy is strong, straight into the critic's message history. The critic rubber-stamps it, because it's reading the generator's self-congratulation, not just the copy.

contentSections.question: The system prompt is properly adversarial. What's still wrong?

options.label: It passes generatorMessages into the critic's context — the critic inherits the generator's own reasoning about the copy despite having a separate system prompt
Nothing — the adversarial system prompt is what matters, the message history is just extra context

feedback.leaked-context: Right. A good adversarial system prompt doesn't survive being handed the generator's own justification for why the copy is good — the critic now has the generator's framing sitting right there in context, which is exactly the same-source problem this whole module opened with, just moved into a function that looks structurally separate.
feedback.fine: The system prompt sets the *instruction*, but the message history is what the model actually reasons over — handing the critic the generator's own reasoning trail reintroduces the shared premises that an independent critic is supposed to avoid.

contentSections.flawExplanation: "Separate call" only buys independence if the call is actually given a clean context. Passing the generator's conversation history into the critic's messages — even with a different system prompt on top — hands the critic the same assumptions the generator formed while writing, undermining the one thing that made the critic worth having.

contentSections.body: A critic is only independent if its call is structurally clean — no conversation history from the generator leaking in, even under a properly adversarial system prompt.

title: Checks that cost less than the mistake
description: Sizing a verification step against what the mistake it would catch actually costs — because a critic call on every step of a 40-step agent is real latency and real money spent on some steps that never needed it.

learningObjectives.text: Weigh the cost of adding a verification step against the cost of the mistake it would catch
Decide, for a specific step in an agent run, whether a check is worth adding

contentSections.body: A team adds a critic call after every single tool call in a 40-step research agent — file lookups, read-only API calls, everything. Total run time roughly doubles. Total token spend roughly doubles too. Almost every one of those steps was a low-stakes, easily-undone read.

contentSections.scenario: The 40-step agent above adds one critic call after every tool call, with the critic call costing roughly the same tokens and latency as the original call it's checking.
contentSections.question: Roughly what multiplier does this put on the agent's total cost and latency, in the worst case where every step gets a critic call?
contentSections.explanation: Doubling one call into two (the original plus its critic) roughly doubles total cost and latency when applied to every single step — the multiplier scales with how many of the 40 steps actually got a critic call layered on. Applied selectively (only the steps where a mistake would actually be expensive) the same technique costs a small fraction of that, which is the whole point of this lesson: the multiplier isn't fixed, it's a choice about which steps earn the extra call.

contentSections.body:
A verification step has a real, measurable cost: extra latency (a full round trip to the model), extra tokens (a second call's worth), and — for anything staged as a resumable unit — extra complexity in what has to be tracked. None of that is free, and applying it uniformly to every step of a long-running agent is a real tax, not a nuance.

The question that decides whether a specific check is worth it: **what does the mistake this check would catch actually cost, if it goes uncaught?** A read-only lookup that returns a wrong count costs almost nothing — the next step that uses it will very likely surface the discrepancy anyway, and nothing external happened. An email sent to a customer, a payment processed, a record deleted — those costs are real, sometimes irreversible, and often invisible until a person outside the system notices.
A verification step costs real latency and real tokens — worth paying only when the mistake it would catch costs more than that, not as a uniform tax on every step.

contentSections.title: Deciding per step, not per agent

contentSections.body: Two steps in the same agent run: one reads its own scratch notes from three steps ago to decide what to search next (wrong notes cost one extra, cheap search — the agent course-corrects next step for free); the other sends a refund confirmation email to a customer (wrong content costs a real, external, hard-to-undo mistake in front of someone who isn't watching the trace).

contentSections.scenario: Steps from a customer-support agent's run: reading its own prior notes, drafting an internal summary for a teammate, sending a refund confirmation email, and deleting a duplicate ticket.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely justify the cost of an added verification step before proceeding?

items.label: Reading its own scratch notes from earlier in the same run to decide the next action
Drafting an internal summary a teammate will read and can easily correct
Sending a refund confirmation email directly to a customer
Deleting a ticket it believes is a duplicate
Logging an internal metric nobody acts on for hours

explanation.own-notes: Low cost if wrong — a bad read of its own notes tends to surface as a bad next step, which the agent (or the next check point) can catch cheaply, without needing a dedicated verification call here.
explanation.internal-summary: Low cost — a teammate reading a slightly-off internal summary can correct it in seconds; nothing external or irreversible happens if this step is wrong.
explanation.refund-email: Real cost — sent is sent. A wrong amount or wrong customer in a refund confirmation is externally visible, hard to walk back cleanly, and directly affects someone who isn't watching this run.
explanation.delete-ticket: Real cost — deleting the wrong ticket destroys something that may not be recoverable, and "believes is a duplicate" is exactly the kind of confident-but-possibly-wrong judgment a check exists to catch before it's irreversible.
explanation.internal-metric: Low cost — a wrong internal number that nobody acts on urgently has a long window to get corrected before it matters.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern across all five: cost of being wrong scales with how external, how irreversible, and how immediately consequential the step is — not with how important the step feels to the agent's overall task. A verification step earns its cost on the steps where being wrong is expensive to discover and expensive to undo, and is a pure tax everywhere else.

contentSections.body: This is a per-step decision, not a per-agent one — the same agent that skips verification on its own scratch-note reads should very likely add it before the refund email and before the delete. Treat it as a short, explicit question at the point you're deciding whether to add a check: if this step is wrong and nobody catches it, what actually happens, and how hard is it to undo? A check earns its cost only when the honest answer to that question is uncomfortable.
Verification is a per-step decision: worth its cost on external, hard-to-undo, high-consequence actions — and a pure tax on the low-stakes steps most of a long-running agent's work actually is.

title: Design verification for eight agent outputs
description: Eight drills applying this module's full toolkit — specific self-review prompts, independent verification against the artefact, clean critic/worker separation, and cost-sized checks — to new scenarios.

learningObjectives.text: Apply self-review design, independent verification, critic/worker separation, and cost-of-check judgment to new agent-output scenarios

contentSections.body: No new concepts here — this is the same toolkit from the five lessons, run against outputs, critics, and cost trade-offs you haven't seen yet.

The habit worth keeping: before trusting an agent's own verdict on its own work, ask what the check actually inspected, whether it could have inherited the mistake it's supposed to catch, and whether its cost was worth what a miss here would actually cost.

title: Add a real critic step to your agent
description: Add an independent critic to an agent you've already built, and prove it actually works by seeding failures it should catch — not just adding a call and assuming it helps.

learningObjectives.text: Design and build an independent critic step, and demonstrate it catching seeded failures a self-review pass would miss

contentSections.body: Everything in this module was building toward one working thing: a critic step that's demonstrably independent — separate context, adversarial framing, structured output — and demonstrably useful, meaning you can show it catching something a same-context self-review pass wouldn't.

contentSections.title: A critic step that demonstrably rejects bad output
contentSections.brief: Take an agent you've already built (from an earlier module's lab, or a small agent built for this one) that produces some checkable artefact — code, a query, a generated document, a data transform. Add a critic step that is structurally independent (separate call, no shared context with the generator), explicitly adversarial, and produces a structured verdict. Then prove it works: seed at least three deliberately bad versions of the artefact and show the critic catching each one, plus show it correctly passing a genuinely good version.
contentSections.deliverable: The critic's system prompt and calling code, a log showing the critic correctly rejecting each of the three seeded failures (with the specific flaw it named), a log showing it correctly passing a good version without false-flagging it, and a short comparison: the same three seeded failures run through a same-context self-review instead, showing what that setup missed.

stages.title: Pick the artefact and define what 'bad' looks like
stages.instructions: Choose the generator and its output type. Write down, concretely, three specific ways this output can be wrong that matter (not vague ones — name the actual defect, the way lesson one's exercise did for file handles and unvalidated arguments). These become your seeded failures.
stages.checkpoint: Three named, specific failure modes for your artefact — each one something a real generator could plausibly produce.

stages.title: Build the independent critic
stages.instructions: Write the critic as a separate call: no conversation history from the generator, an explicit adversarial system prompt naming the categories of flaw to hunt for, and a structured output (specific flaws tied to specifics, or NONE_FOUND). Wire it in per lesson four's pattern — the critic never sees the generator's own reasoning, only the finished artefact.
stages.checkpoint: A critic call whose context, when you inspect what's actually sent to the model, contains only the artefact — nothing from how it was produced.

stages.title: Seed the failures and prove the critic catches them
stages.instructions: Manually construct or prompt for each of your three seeded bad versions (don't rely on the generator producing a bug by chance — deliberately break it each of the three specific ways you named). Run the critic against each, and against one genuinely good version. Then run the same three bad versions through a same-context self-review setup and record what it catches, for the comparison.
stages.checkpoint: A log showing 3/3 seeded failures caught by the independent critic with specific, correct flaws named, the good version passing cleanly, and a same-context self-review run on the same three failures for comparison.

rubric.criterion: The critic is structurally independent
rubric.meets: The critic's call contains no conversation history or reasoning trail from the generator — only the finished artefact, verifiable by inspecting what's actually sent.

rubric.criterion: The critic's instruction is genuinely adversarial and specific
rubric.meets: The system prompt names concrete categories of flaw to hunt for and assumes one exists, rather than asking an open 'does this look right.'

rubric.criterion: The critic's output is structured and specific
rubric.meets: Flagged flaws are tied to exact locations in the artefact, not a paragraph of general impressions.

rubric.criterion: The seeded failures are genuine, named defects
rubric.meets: Each of the three failures is a specific, concrete way the artefact can be wrong — not a vague 'make it worse.'

rubric.criterion: The critic demonstrably catches what it should, and doesn't false-flag good output
rubric.meets: All three seeded failures are caught with correct, specific reasons; the good version passes without a false flag.

rubric.criterion: The comparison against same-context self-review is honest
rubric.meets: The same three failures run through same-context self-review, with the actual result reported — including if it also happened to catch some of them, not just the cases favoring the critic.

contentSections.body: A critic step earns the extra call by being structurally independent, genuinely adversarial, and specific — and the only way to know it actually works is to seed real failures and watch it catch them, not assume it does because it looks like a check.

title: Checkpoint — Self-Checking
description: Ungraded retrieval: 4 from this module, 4 from Choosing an Approach (the previous module in the track), 2 from further back in Decomposition.

learningObjectives.text: Recall this module's verification vocabulary and reconnect it to the strategy-selection module that precedes it

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — Self-Checking
contentSections.framing: No grade, no timer. Answer from memory before scrolling back.

questions.prompt: Why does same-context self-review tend to just agree with the output it's reviewing?

options.label: It reasons from the same premises that produced the mistake, and models default toward agreeable, confirming responses unless explicitly pushed to find fault
The model isn't capable of finding its own mistakes
Self-review only works on code, not on other kinds of output

questions.explanation: Lesson two's SQL example showed the same model catching far more of the same bugs once given a fresh context and an adversarial framing — the capability was there, the setup wasn't.

questions.prompt: What makes a verification step genuinely independent rather than a narrative re-check?

options.label: It executes the actual artefact against real or fixture data and compares the real output to a known expectation
It asks the model to re-read its own explanation and confirm it matches the request
It runs on a different day than the generation step

questions.explanation: Lesson three's schema-conversion example: comparing a description to a description never executes the work. Running the artefact and diffing real output against a real expectation produces a fact independent of anyone's belief about it.

questions.prompt: A critic call has its own adversarial system prompt, but the code passes it the generator's full conversation history as context. Is it independent?

options.label: No — the shared context reintroduces the generator's own reasoning and assumptions, undermining the independence the separate prompt was meant to create
Yes — a different system prompt is what makes a call a critic, regardless of what else is in its context

questions.explanation: Lesson four's spot-flaw showed exactly this leak — a properly adversarial prompt doesn't survive being handed the generator's own justification for why the output is good.

questions.prompt: What's the actual question that decides whether a specific step deserves a verification check?

options.label: What does it cost, in practice, if this step is wrong and nobody catches it — and how hard is that to undo?
Whether the step feels important to the agent's overall task
Whether a verification step is cheap enough to add everywhere

questions.explanation: Lesson five's evidence-stack contrasted a refund email and a ticket deletion (real, external, hard-to-undo cost) against reading one's own scratch notes (cheap to be wrong about) — the deciding factor was consequence and reversibility, not how central the step felt.

questions.prompt: Why run cheap checks before committing to an expensive approach, per that module's lesson on the subject?

options.label: A cheap check can rule out or validate an assumption the expensive approach depends on, before spending the larger cost
Cheap checks are always more accurate than expensive ones
There's no real reason — it's just a convention

questions.explanation: The same cost-sizing instinct as this module's last lesson: spend the larger cost only once a smaller one has told you it's likely to pay off.

questions.prompt: What does recording why an approach was chosen actually protect against, per that module?

options.label: A later reviewer (human or another agent call) re-litigating a decision with no memory of what was already ruled out and why
Nothing concrete — it's mostly a documentation nicety
Only protects against the original agent forgetting its own reasoning mid-run

questions.explanation: Worth reconnecting here: a critic reviewing an artefact with no record of why the approach behind it was chosen is set up to flag decisions that were already deliberately made, wasting the exact independence this module spent four lessons building.

questions.prompt: What's the risk in generating only one candidate approach and going with it?

options.label: The first approach a model produces is whatever pattern is most statistically likely to come next, not necessarily the best one for this specific situation
There's no risk — models are trained to produce the best approach first
It only matters for creative tasks, not technical ones

questions.explanation: The same lesson this module opened with, one level up: a single pass — whether it's the first approach or the first self-review — reflects one reasoning path, not a deliberately checked one.

questions.prompt: What makes a good "abandon this approach" signal, versus persisting past the point it's worth it?

options.label: A concrete, pre-stated condition — a cost threshold, a specific failure repeating — decided before starting, not a vague sense that it's taking too long
Whichever approach has consumed the most effort so far, since abandoning it would waste that effort
Waiting for the approach to fail completely before considering an alternative

questions.explanation: The sunk-cost trap this guards against is the same shape as this module's checks-cost-less-than-the-mistake framing: decide the threshold before you're emotionally or computationally invested in the answer.

questions.prompt: What's the test for whether two steps in a plan are genuinely safe to run concurrently?

options.label: No data flow between them, and no shared mutable state — both, not just the first
Neither step reads the other's return value
They appear next to each other in the plan

questions.explanation: Worth reconnecting here because both modules share a deeper pattern: a check that looks sufficient on the surface (no data flow; a system prompt that sounds adversarial) can still miss a real dependency (shared state; leaked context) that only shows up on close inspection.

questions.prompt: What three properties make a plan step's completion condition genuinely checkable?

options.label: A concrete target, a mechanical check, and a binary answer
A clear description and a confident tone
Approval from the model that wrote the step

questions.explanation: The same three properties this module's independent-verification lesson leans on directly: a real check needs a concrete target and a mechanical way to resolve it, not a model's opinion of its own work.

contentSections.body: If these mostly landed, you can tell a genuine check from a check-shaped restatement — the skill this whole module was built to teach, and the one the next module's adaptation work depends on when a check reveals the plan was wrong.

title: The plan meets the actual environment
description: Every plan is built on assumptions about the world it will run in — and the gap between those assumptions and what's actually true is where a good plan starts producing bad results.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the specific assumptions a plan is implicitly relying on about its environment
Explain why a well-formed plan can still fail purely because the world changed underneath it

contentSections.title: Every plan is a bet on the world staying still

contentSections.body: An agent's plan to migrate a customer's billing assumes the customer has exactly one active subscription — true when the plan was written, an hour before it ran. In that hour, the customer's sales rep added a second subscription for an add-on product. The plan is well-formed, every step checkable, every dependency correct. It also silently migrates the wrong subscription, because the world it was built for isn't the world it ran in.

contentSections.scenario: Three things baked into the billing-migration plan without anyone writing them down: (1) the customer has exactly one active subscription, (2) the pricing API's response shape hasn't changed since the plan was tested, (3) the migration will run before the customer's next billing cycle.
contentSections.question: What are these three things, structurally?

options.label: Unstated assumptions the plan depends on being true, even though nothing in the plan checks them
Bugs in the plan that should have been caught by a plan review

feedback.assumptions: Right. None of these are errors in the plan's logic — the steps are correctly sequenced and each has a checkable completion condition. They're facts about the world the plan-writer took for granted, and a plan built on them is only as good as those facts staying true between when the plan was made and when it executes.
