contentSections.body: Everything in this module was building toward one working thing: not just a multi-agent system, but proof it earned its complexity — a real comparison, on the same task, against the single-agent version it's replacing, with both the cost multiplier and the quality difference actually measured rather than assumed.

contentSections.title: A two-agent system, measured against its single-agent alternative
contentSections.brief: Pick a task with a genuine structural reason for two agents, per lesson one — a real context-capacity limit, a real need for independent judgment applied twice, or genuinely parallel independent sub-tasks. Build a single-agent baseline first. Then build the two-agent version (orchestrator/worker, or generator/independent-critic, or two genuinely independent parallel agents — whichever structure fits your chosen reason) with a clean, structured handoff between the roles. Run both versions on the same set of at least 8 test cases and measure cost (calls, tokens, latency) and quality (a concrete measure specific to your task) for each.
contentSections.deliverable: A one-paragraph justification of the specific structural reason two agents were needed here (per lesson one's checklist), both agents' code and prompts, the handoff format between them, results from both the single-agent and two-agent versions run on the same ≥8 test cases, a table comparing measured cost multiplier and measured quality difference, and an honest verdict on whether the multiplier was worth the quality gain for this specific use case.

stages.title: Pick the task and justify the structural need
stages.instructions: Choose a task and identify which specific structural reason from lesson one justifies two agents for it — not a vague sense that it would be better. Build and run the single-agent baseline on your test cases first, recording its cost and quality.
stages.checkpoint: A written justification naming the specific structural reason, plus baseline single-agent results on at least 8 test cases.

stages.title: Build the two-agent version with a clean handoff
stages.instructions: Build the second agent (worker, critic, or parallel peer, matching your chosen structure) with a narrowly scoped prompt per lesson two, and design the handoff between the two roles per lesson three — structured working material, not a vague summary and not the full raw process. If your design is a second-opinion setup, apply lesson four's independence test: something structural has to actually differ between the two agents.
stages.checkpoint: A working two-agent pipeline whose handoff, inspected directly, contains the receiving agent's actual working material.

stages.title: Run both versions on the same cases and measure honestly
stages.instructions: Run the two-agent version on the exact same test cases as the baseline. Record calls, tokens, and latency for both. Score quality with a concrete, specific measure for your task (not a vague impression) for both versions. Build the comparison table and write the verdict: was the measured multiplier worth the measured quality gain, for this specific use case's actual cost of an uncaught mistake?
stages.checkpoint: A comparison table with real numbers on both sides, and a verdict that engages honestly with whether the trade was worth it — including if the answer is no.

rubric.criterion: The need for two agents is a genuine structural reason
rubric.meets: The justification names a specific capacity limit, independence need, or real parallelism — not a vague sense that two agents would help.

rubric.criterion: Each role is narrowly scoped
rubric.meets: Each agent's job is describable in one sentence without 'and also,' with no responsibility bleeding across roles.

rubric.criterion: The handoff carries real working material
rubric.meets: The handoff format, inspected directly, contains specific facts/results the receiving agent needs — not a vague summary and not the full raw process of the sending agent.

rubric.criterion: Any independence claim is genuine, not cosmetic
rubric.meets: If the design relies on independent judgment, something structural (framing, examples, or model) actually differs between the two agents — not just surface wording.

rubric.criterion: Cost and quality are both measured, not assumed
rubric.meets: Real numbers — calls, tokens, latency, and a concrete quality measure — exist for both the single-agent and two-agent versions on the same test cases.

rubric.criterion: The final verdict is honest
rubric.meets: The verdict weighs the measured multiplier against the measured gain and the actual cost of an uncaught mistake for this use case — including reporting a negative verdict if the trade genuinely isn't worth it.

contentSections.body: A two-agent system earns its place the same way a verification check does: a real structural reason it's needed, roles scoped to do one job each, a handoff that actually carries what's needed, genuine rather than cosmetic independence, and a measured comparison against the simpler alternative — not an architecture diagram that assumes more agents means better.

title: Checkpoint — More Than One Agent
description: Ungraded retrieval: 4 from this module, 4 from Adapting to Reality (the previous module in the track), 2 from further back in Self-Checking.

learningObjectives.text: Recall this module's multi-agent vocabulary and reconnect it to the adaptation module that precedes it

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — More Than One Agent
contentSections.framing: No grade, no timer. Answer from memory before scrolling back.

questions.from: This module — More Than One Agent
questions.prompt: "The output isn't good enough yet" — is this a genuine structural reason to add a second agent?

options.label: No — it's usually a prompt, sourcing, or model-choice problem, and a second badly-specified agent doesn't fix a badly-specified first one
Yes — more agents reliably improves output quality
Yes, but only if the second agent uses a bigger model

questions.explanation: Lesson one's thin-summaries example: adding agents around a badly-specified single agent duplicates the same underlying cause rather than fixing it.

questions.from: This module — More Than One Agent
questions.prompt: What should a worker's system prompt in an orchestrator-worker pipeline know about the other workers?

options.label: Nothing — it should be scoped to its own sub-task, with consistency coming from a shared output format the orchestrator enforces
It should know how many other workers exist, to produce more comparable output
It should know the other workers' results, to avoid duplicating effort

questions.explanation: Lesson two's concept-flow: awareness of siblings adds nothing to a worker's actual job and risks it reasoning about a pipeline it can't see or coordinate with.

questions.from: This module — More Than One Agent
questions.prompt: A handoff between two agents includes the sending agent's entire raw process — every tool call and dead end. What's the actual problem, given nothing is technically lost?

options.label: The relevant facts are diluted across volume the receiving agent has to weigh equally, which is a real attention cost even without a hard context overflow
Nothing — more information handed off is always safer than less
The context window will always overflow with this much material

questions.explanation: Lesson three's diagnose-mechanism: this is a signal-to-noise cost, not a capacity failure — the receiving agent has to do extraction work the handoff should have already done.

questions.from: This module — More Than One Agent
questions.prompt: Two agents given identical prompts, inputs, and examples agree 39/40 times. What does that agreement rate actually measure?

options.label: How similar their setups are, not how correct their shared conclusion is — they're one reasoning process run twice
Strong, independent validation that the shared conclusion is correct
Nothing meaningful, since agreement rates are never informative

questions.explanation: Lesson four's mechanism: this is the same-context self-review problem from the previous module, reappearing at the multi-agent scale — shared premises produce shared conclusions regardless of whether those premises are correct.

questions.prompt: What decides whether the right response to a wrong assumption is a local adaptation or a full restart?

options.label: How far the wrong assumption's actual consequences reach through the plan's steps — traced, not guessed
How foundational or embarrassing the wrong assumption feels
How long the plan had already been running before the discovery

questions.explanation: The same tracing discipline this module uses to decide whether a second agent is genuinely needed rather than just added by reflex.

questions.prompt: How should you find the boundary between still-valid and stale partial work in an interrupted batch?

options.label: From real evidence — a version field, a timestamp, or sampled comparison against the current standard — not a guessed round number
Reprocess a conservative-sounding round number to be safe
Trust every item's individual completion flag as proof it's still valid

questions.explanation: Worth reconnecting here: this module's cost-multiplier lesson leans on the same evidence-over-assumption discipline — measure the real numbers rather than assuming a multi-agent system is worth its cost.

questions.prompt: What does a genuinely useful adaptation report need to name, beyond just the end state?

options.label: The specific assumption that broke, the specific action taken because of it, and what's still uncertain going forward
Just a confirmation that the task completed successfully
An apology for the plan needing to change

questions.explanation: The same specificity standard this module's honest-verdict lesson applies to a multi-agent system's cost comparison — real numbers and a named trade-off, not a summary that assumes the outcome was good.

questions.prompt: A step fails with an error that's a stable fact about the world rather than a temporary condition. What should NOT happen next?

options.label: Retrying the identical call with backoff, since it will fail identically every time
Tracing the error to the specific assumption it contradicts
Checking how far that broken assumption's consequences reach through the rest of the plan

questions.explanation: Worth reconnecting here — the same instinct to check whether an approach's premise still holds, rather than mechanically repeating it, is what this module applies to deciding whether a second agent's setup is genuinely independent or just repeating the first agent's reasoning.

questions.prompt: What makes a critic call structurally independent from the generator whose work it's reviewing?

options.label: A separate call with no shared conversation history from the generator, plus an explicit adversarial instruction and a structured output
Using a more detailed system prompt in the same conversation
Asking the generator to grade its own confidence

questions.explanation: The exact template this module's independence lesson reused for peer agents instead of a critic/generator pair — clean context and something structurally different are both required.

questions.prompt: What's the actual question that decides whether a specific step deserves a verification check?

options.label: What does it cost, in practice, if this step is wrong and nobody catches it — and how hard is that to undo?
Whether the step feels important to the agent's overall task
Whether the check is cheap enough to add everywhere

questions.explanation: The same question, one level up, decides this module's cost-multiplier lesson: what does an uncaught mistake cost in this specific use case, weighed against the measured multiplier a second agent adds.

contentSections.body: If these mostly landed, you can tell a genuine reason for a second agent from a reflex, scope roles narrowly, hand off real working material, build actual independence, and price what it costs — the full toolkit this phase built, from decomposing one agent's work through coordinating several.
